body: At seven, at the Delgado front desk, Theo had informed the lobby that Mr. Arceneaux would be staying with them. “The Sandpiper had bedbugs.” “The Sandpiper had a *vacancy*,” Lena said. “And bedbugs,” said Theo. “I called.” Wes, the empty jar under his arm, only grinned. “Free is free, dawlin’.” Up in 412 an Aerobed waited in its box, bought that afternoon “for guests.” Taped to the counter, beside the pen on its bead chain:

body.title: Laminated, the front desk
body.text:
OVERNIGHT GUESTS: REGISTER BY 10 P.M.
THREE NIGHTS MAXIMUM.
THIS MEANS YOU.
—P. Raman, RA

body: Wes signed for Friday, Saturday and Sunday in a slow, round hand, and hung the pen back on its chain.

Shipwreck Cove, at ten past nine, belongs to Laney. She promised Lena a fire every Friday, and she keeps her promises in lighter fluid: driftwood and two broken pallets in the ring of black rocks, burning high and loud, the sparks climbing the bluff toward the stairs and the dead Christmas lights along the rail, dark as a necklace in a drawer. Past the fire the schooner’s ribs stand up out of the sand, lit on the near side and gone on the far. No moon. More stars over the water than seems strictly reasonable, and the surf out there in the dark, loud and invisible. Down the beach Pi Lam has a fire of its own and is shrieking at it.

Everybody is on the logs. Kevin, in a navy quarter-zip, feeds the fire on a schedule only he knows. Margot has the one folding chair, because she brought it. Theo has the 5D in his lap with the lens cap on, for once, and is watching Wes. Becca is beside Jack. And on the far side of the fire, against Wes, with his Tulane sweatshirt pulled down over her hands, Lena.

Becca has brought s’mores. She has brought them in gallon Ziplocs labeled in marker on strips of masking tape: GRAHAMS. HERSHEY’S. MARSHMALLOWS (NEW BAG). STICKS (WASHED). Laney lowers her Solo cup to read the tape. “She labeled the marshmallows.”
“Laney. Be nice.”
“So nobody gets the stale ones!” says Becca, delighted to be asked, and hands Laney a stick. Washed. Laney takes it.

Laney’s iPod dock sits on the cooler, and Taylor Swift is working her way through “Love Story” toward the part with the ring. Margot raises both eyebrows at the cooler and holds them up through the key change.

And Wes is easy. Jack came down the stairs with a whole plan for disliking him, and it doesn’t make it to the sand. Wes talks Saints the way Nonna talks saints: who did what, and when, and what it cost. “Worst Sunday of the year, podna. Four and oh and nobody to play.” He was in the Dome last Sunday for Sharper — “ninety-nine yards, Ohio, and he was laughing by the fifty” — and in 1980, nine years before Wes was born, his daddy and Mr. Tony Broussard went to the Dome with paper bags over their heads. “One and fifteen. My daddy still has his bag. Mama won’t let it in the house.”

“We had our own bag,” Jack says. “It was the whole city.” The Browns are oh and four. Wes wants to know who’s playing quarterback. “That’s the question,” Jack says. “Anderson or Quinn. It’s been the question since August. The answer is no.”

Then, without either of them finding the turn, it’s levees and Lordstown. “The Corps built them wrong,” Wes says, poking the fire with Kevin’s stick. “I’m gonna build them right.” And Jack, who doesn’t say this to people, says it to him: twenty-six years on the line, Cavaliers and then Cobalts, laid off since June, a list at the union hall for the new small car. “Next year, maybe.” Wes’s daddy has welded hulls at Avondale for thirty years, and he says *Avondale* the way Jack says *Lordstown*. Both their fathers built things with their hands. Jack notices it, and takes the marshmallow Becca is holding out to him, and lets it go.
“He thanked me for the sign,” Theo tells Jack, low, the way you’d report a crime. “He *kept* the sign.”

Margot, from her chair, cross-examines Wes on the Army Corps of Engineers: the 17th Street Canal, the London Avenue Canal, who designed the floodwalls, who signed off, and who, specifically, still has a job. Wes answers slowly, with names and years, and twice says, “I don’t know, and that’s a problem.” Margot sits back. To Jack, not lowering her voice much: “He’s the first man in this saga I’d let carry my bag.”

By then Becca and Wes have found each other: his mama in Gentilly, who has never let a living soul leave her house without a plate; her seven. They are, it turns out, both the one who plans the thing. Becca has her clipboard on her knee, and *Saints* is already checked off.

body.text: Somewhere in there Becca stands up on her log, both arms high, and gives the cove a “WHO DAT!” in her best cattle-call voice. Down the beach Pi Lam answers with something wordless. Wes is beside himself. “Who taught you that?” “Jack!”
body.else: Somewhere in there Becca tries a “who dat” at the fire, politely, like a question, and Wes gets up off his log to teach her the arm.

journal.title: Wes Arceneaux
journal.text: Lena’s boyfriend. Tulane, civil engineering; the boat at sixteen. Six-two, a chipped front tooth, a Saints cap he’s been bending since 2006. Calls me the Ohio guy. Says she called me a jagoff and that means she likes me; he’s known her since she had a retainer. Drank the Pacific: the jar came back empty. Theo fetched him from the airport alone, in a two-seater, with a sign, and cancelled his motel. Bedbugs, Theo says. He’s on Theo’s new air mattress in our room, three nights. The Corps built the walls wrong; he’s going to build them right. I like him.

response: “Tell me about the levees,” Jack says, and Wes looks at him across the fire to see if he means it, and he does. So Wes tells him. The floodwalls on the canals were concrete I-walls set on steel sheet pile, and the sheet pile wasn’t driven deep enough into soft ground, peat and sand and old swamp, and when the water came up in the canals the walls didn’t go over the top. They went *out*. The London Avenue Canal broke two blocks from his mama’s.
“Everybody thinks it was the water,” Wes says. “Water does what water does. A wall’s only as good as what it’s standing in.”

Wes laughs the big laugh, the whole-body one, and nearly goes off the back of his log, and then the two of them are gone: Brees and Anderson, the Dome and the Dawg Pound, 1980 and every year since 1999. Becca asks what a Dawg Pound is and gets two answers at once, Wes’s about dogs and Jack’s about dog biscuits and D-cell batteries, and decides she likes Jack’s better.
Wes looks at the fire. It isn’t long. Then, easy, the tooth showing: “Another night, Ohio.”
And he turns to Becca and asks her about horses, and Becca, who has *horses??* written on a clipboard under his name, is overjoyed to tell him.

s04b.slug: FRIDAY · 9:52 PM · SHIPWRECK COVE, BY THE RIBS

body.text: At ten to ten Wes digs a scuffed black flip phone out of his jeans, holds it close to his face to find what he wants, and props it open on top of Laney’s dock where the iPod was. A fiddle saws out of it, thin and sweet, and a dead man’s voice crying something in French. “Lena’s Mémère makes everybody learn it,” Wes tells Becca, and holds out his hand to Lena. “Come on, dawlin’.”
body.else: At ten to ten Wes digs a scuffed black flip phone out of his jeans and props it open on Laney’s dock. A fiddle saws out of it, thin and sweet, a dead man singing in French. “‘Jolie Blonde,’” he tells Becca. “Lena’s Mémère makes everybody learn it.” He waltzes Lena by the ribs, bouncing, and she laughs at him.

body.text: He waltzes her by the ribs. Jack knows the song. He knows the sand too: eight nights ago, a few yards from where Wes is turning her now, he learned this, long, short, short, with his hand at her back and the moon on the water. Tonight there’s no moon, only the fire on one side and the black timbers on the other. Wes bounces. Cajuns don’t bounce; Jack has this on authority. Over Wes’s shoulder Lena’s face comes round with the turn, and finds the ribs, and comes back.
body.else: Then Becca has Jack up by both hands — “I can’t sit through a fiddle, it’s physically impossible” — and since he doesn’t know the waltz she teaches him a country two-step instead, in the sand, counting out loud, *quick, quick, slow, slow*. Nobody asks him anything.

body.text: Then Becca has him up by both hands. “Come on. I can’t sit through a waltz, it’s physically impossible.” She puts his right hand where it goes and takes his left, and counts him in under her breath, and on the first long step it turns out he doesn’t need counting. Long, short, short. His feet have it before he does. Becca leans back to look at them, thrilled. “Jack. Where’d you learn *that*?”
Over Lena’s head, across the firelight, Wes’s face is turned their way. He is waiting for the answer too.

choices.key: At the bonfire Becca asked where you learned the waltz. You told her: Lena.
response: “Lena taught me,” Jack says.

“She’s so *nice*!” says Becca, as if this settles something wonderful. And Wes, laughing, over the fiddle and Lena’s hair: “She taught me too. Tenth grade. I bounce.” He says it warm. The song winds down on one long sawing note, and the four of them come back to the logs, Becca still counting under her breath.

choices.key: At the bonfire Becca asked where you learned the waltz. You said Youngstown weddings.
response: “Youngstown weddings,” Jack says. “Cookie tables and polkas. You can’t get out of a reception on the South Side alive without it.”

Becca believes him at once, and loves it. “We have a Polish wedding every summer at St. Pius! Every summer! The Nowaks!” Lena, on the turn, has heard; Jack sees her eyes go to the fire. Then the song ends, and they’re all back on the logs, and Becca is telling Wes everything about the Nowaks.

choices.key: At the bonfire Becca asked where you learned the waltz. You said YouTube.
response: “YouTube,” Jack says.

Becca takes it at face value, gladly. “You can learn *anything* on there! Eli rebuilt a carburetor off of YouTube.” Wes laughs. Lena doesn’t, quite. The fiddle saws its last and quits, and the four of them troop back to the logs, Becca already listing what she’s going to look up.

response.text: He doesn’t answer. He turns her instead, and Becca lets the question go — she’s counting now under her breath, *one, two, three*, grinning down at her own Ropers — and over her shoulder Wes’s eyes stay on Jack until the turn takes him the other way.
response.else: He keeps his mouth shut and his eyes on his feet, and still steps on her Ropers twice, and she forgives him both times out loud: “Forgiven! Forgiven.”

response: Then the song ends, and the four of them are back on the logs.

body: At twenty-five to eleven Laney gets up, walks all the way around the fire, and puts the big yellow Maglite out of Kevin’s glove box into Jack’s hand. “Now, Shakespeare.”

Theo’s lens cap comes off. The 5D comes up. Laney has her pink BlackBerry out too, held sideways, the little red light on. Kevin shuts his eyes. “Respectfully,” he says, “this is a hostage situation.”

body.text: Jack hasn’t agreed to anything. It doesn’t matter. Laney turns to the fire, to the whole cove and a fair amount of the Pacific, and puts on the pageant voice. “Y’all. Jack has something he’d like to share with us.” Every face comes round.

body: The napkin is in his back pocket against Hale’s Williams, where it has been since lunch. He couldn’t do her eyes. He tried, through the long wait in the lot for Theo, and he didn’t know them, and he isn’t going to guess. So he did her freckles instead, from memory, on both sides of the napkin, in the shape of the Hopkins he sent to Trumbull a week ago Thursday — the copy Lena erased her own name out of.

body.title: A Fishbowl napkin, both sides

body: He clicks the Maglite on and reads the first line out loud. “Glory be to God for freckled things —”

Becca doesn’t cover her freckles. She never has. They’re all over her in the firelight: nose, cheekbones, the backs of her hands around the clipboard. Laney, whose freckles live under foundation, has stopped filming. Across the fire, at *freckled*, Lena looks down into the flames. She knows the poem underneath this one; she spent an hour in the laundry room helping him erase his pencil out of the book it came from.
The rest of it is in his hand.

choices.text: Read it — and finish on one knee, the way Laney said.
choices.key: At the bonfire you read Becca a poem about her freckles and finished it on one knee. “Not yet, Jack Costigan.”
response: He reads it, all of it, both sides, the light jumping on the lines, and on *Praise him* he goes down in the sand on one knee in front of her, the way Laney said, and looks up. Her eyes are gray. He has never once seen it.

Then the cove screams. Laney screams, Kevin says “*No*,” Pi Lam screams from down the beach without the faintest idea why, and Becca’s hands fly to her mouth, and for one second her whole face is pure hope. “OHIO!” Wes whoops. Lena has gone still.
“It’s *Hopkins*!” Jack says from the sand. “It’s a poem!”

Becca gets her hands down and her ranch back. “Not yet, Jack Costigan.” And she bends and kisses him, quick, on the mouth, in front of the fire and God and Pi Lam. “So there’s no confusion,” she says. “That was a *poem*.”

When the noise comes down Theo lowers the 5D. “Halloween,” he announces across the fire. “Mine. I’ve rented a house.” “Jack!” says Becca, who hasn’t let go of his sleeve. “We should *match*!” Near midnight they climb the switchbacks past the dark Christmas lights, the moon just up over the hills, low and lopsided, Wes’s arm around Lena and Becca’s hand in Jack’s. On the third landing Wes leans back over the rail. “Ohio,” he says, “you’re a madman.”

After two, in 412, in the dark, Wes lies on the Aerobed in Theo’s Meridian Pictures robe, and Theo is asleep or doing a fair impression. “She’s good people,” Wes says. “Your Becca.” Then something about the Saints’ secondary, and he’s asleep in the middle of it.

journal.title: Laney’s advice
journal.text: Laney Price, on romance: a poem, out loud, at a bonfire, about her eyes. It has to rhyme. And then — this is the important part — one knee. Never again. I did the knee. Becca said: Not yet.

journal.title: Becca Lindell
journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer — elk too. Has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Asked about the scar in the water. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Wrote FRIDAY? on her clipboard, and meant it. Drives her brother Eli’s red Ranger; St. Isidore on the visor. Second date: Friday-night football. Knows downs. Prayed a Glory Be on fourth and one. Learned the First Way on the bleachers and said it back perfectly. Kissed my cheek so there’s no confusion. Third date was mine. I asked. I paid. The elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset, in Kevin’s Odyssey. She knew what every one of them weighed. Nobody’s ever planned a thing for her, she says. She’s been praying for two in the morning. Named a hermit crab Thomas, after the First Way, and asked Fr. Osei whose blessing it was. Works the Marine Lab touch tank Thursday afternoons and Friday at six in the morning — that’s how she signed Thomas out. He’s home; she knows him by the chip in his shell. Mailed Rosie a birthday card with Thomas on it and six true facts on the back, to the address I gave her for her Christmas cards. She does them in October. Has a page on her clipboard for Wes. She’s been praying for him and Lena since September. Her eyes are gray.

choices.text: Read it standing up, to her, and sit back down.
choices.key: At the bonfire you read Becca a poem about her freckles, standing, to her, and sat back down.
response: He reads it standing, to her — not to the fire, not to the camera — the light jumping on the napkin, and at the last line he looks up off the paper and sees that her eyes are gray. He hadn’t known. He sits back down on the log beside her.

For a second there’s nothing but the fire going and the surf out in the dark. Lena claps first. Then everybody, Wes loudest. Becca has both hands pressed together under her chin. “Will you write it down for me?” “It’s written down,” Jack says, and gives her the napkin, and she folds it in four and buttons it into the chest pocket of her Carhartt vest.

Theo caps the lens. “Halloween,” he announces across the fire. “Mine. I’ve rented a house.” “Jack!” says Becca. “We should *match*!” Near midnight they climb the switchbacks past the dark Christmas lights, the moon just up over the hills, low and lopsided, Wes’s arm around Lena and Becca’s hand in Jack’s, her other hand flat on the buttoned pocket.

s05.slug: SATURDAY · 12:25 PM · THE MADONNA INN, SAN LUIS OBISPO
body: Saturday morning, in order: Wes made the Aerobed with hospital corners — nobody in 412 has ever done that to anything — and then stood a long time in front of Rosie’s drawing on the wall over Jack’s desk, a yellow sun and a red thing with a great many legs. “Who drew the spider?” “It’s a crab.” “Sure it is.” By nine Kevin had the real tire back on the Odyssey — the Chevron on Mission, seventy-five cents of air — and reported, twice, that there is nothing wrong with it. And under every door on the fourth floor and the second, on heavy cream stock, this:

body.title: Meridian Pictures letterhead
body.text:
THE COLUMBUS DAY EXPEDITION
Saturday, October 10, 2009

11:00 — Departure (Anacapa lot)
12:15 — Landfall
12:30 — Pink champagne cake (lunch is a social construct)
2:00 — Entertainment (Miss Price)
4:00 — Return voyage

Dress: festive. Questions: no.
—T.A.V.

body: At eleven, in the Anacapa lot, Laney has a seating chart. It isn’t written down. It doesn’t need to be. “Guests ride up front,” she says, steering Wes by the elbow to the passenger door of the Odyssey. “It’s *manners*.” She takes the middle row with Margot, who buckles in and opens a notebook — “I’m studying a cargo cult” — and before Kevin is out of the lot Laney has one hand up over the seat back, not turning around, until Lena puts her oatmeal cardigan in it. “Air-conditioning,” Laney says. “I *know* these places.” Which leaves the way back for Jack and Lena.

Fifty minutes up the 101, through Santa Maria and over the hill to Pismo, with Wes’s laugh coming back over the seats every couple of miles at something Kevin said. Lena sits against her window with her knees drawn up and watches the strawberry fields go by, row on row. Jack has the Williams open on his knee to a page he doesn’t turn. Margot glances back once, at the two of them, and returns to her notebook. “Columbus made landfall on the twelfth,” she says, without looking up. “Leif Erikson beat him by five hundred years and had the decency not to write it up.”

Becca drives the SL. Theo offered in the lot, held out the keys to his grandfather’s car as if it cost him nothing, and Becca looked at the dash — “’79, four-fifty, that’s a V8” — and got in. When the van pulls into the Madonna Inn lot she’s parked, top down, and out, stretching. Theo is still in the passenger seat with his sunglasses pushed up into his hair, looking straight ahead, reverent. “Nobody drives my grandfather’s car,” he tells Jack quietly, over the door.

Jack has been warned about the Madonna Inn, and it is pinker than the warning. The walls are boulders, actual boulders, mortared into a Swiss-chalet fever dream beside the freeway; the lampposts are pink, the sugar packets are pink, the carpet is a pink so committed it seems to be making a point. The Gold Rush Steak House has round booths of hot-pink tufted leather big enough for a parish council, and in the middle of the room a tree made all of gold, as pleased with itself as a cat. Dean Martin is coming out of the ceiling. The cake arrives pink, with pink chocolate curls.

Wes vanishes downstairs and comes back up halfway, to the turn of the stairs, with his cap pushed back. “Ohio,” he says. “Ohio, come look at this.” The men’s room is green tile and clamshell sinks and, along one whole wall, a waterfall coming down over rock — and the waterfall is the urinal. Wes stands in front of it with his hands on his hips. “Somebody had to *design* this,” he says, in deep professional respect. “Somebody stamped the drawings.”
Back at the booth Theo has a fork in the champagne cake and isn’t eating it. “She brought me every summer,” he says. “My grandmother. She said it was vulgar. She ordered two pieces.”
Then he’s Theo again. He catches the waitress by the elbow, the Rolex winking. “Another for the table,” he says. “On Meridian.”

s05b.slug: SATURDAY · 2:05 PM · THE MADONNA INN, A PINK BOOTH
body: By two the cake is a ruin of pink crumbs and the booth is a game show. Laney is up on her knees on the hot-pink leather in Lena’s oatmeal cardigan, sleeves shoved to the elbow, the cake knife held to her mouth like a microphone and a stack of index cards in her other hand, already written, in purple. “And our next contestants,” she says, in full pageant-host, “from the great state of *Idaho* —”

Becca waves to an audience of six. Theo is the network: the 5D propped among the coffee cups, recording. Margot is standards and practices. Kevin has a napkin and a pen and has appointed himself the judges, scoring on a system he declines to disclose, which awards points for accuracy, enthusiasm and once, inexplicably, penmanship. The contestants are Jack and Becca, and Wes and Lena.

Laney reads the first card — “Where was your first —” — and Margot looks at her. That is all Margot does. The card goes face down on the table, and Laney picks up the next one without dropping her smile.

Becca on Jack. *What’s in his back pocket?* Becca doesn’t even look at the card. “A book. This week it’s *Moral Luck* by Bernard Williams, and it’s not his, it’s Professor Hale’s, and he owes him notes in it. He told me at the fish place in Cambria.” Laney turns Jack’s card over. It says the same thing in fewer words. Correct to the comma.
Jack on Becca. *Her favorite animal?* “Cows?” Becca’s card: HORSES (OBVIOUSLY). She laughs, with no edge in it anywhere. “He studies me like a test,” she tells the booth, “and still fails.”
Jack on Becca. *Her eye color?* “Gray,” Jack says. Becca glows. Laney says something into the cake knife that the network doesn’t catch.

Then Laney turns to Wes, and the voice goes up half a step. *Lena’s favorite saint?* Wes leans back in the pink leather with his arm along the top of the booth behind Lena, smiling, sure of it. Jack knows the answer.

body.text: He has known it since the first Tuesday of the semester, in Sandoval Hall, when Margot called Catherine of Siena Lena’s exemplar and Lena turned around in her seat to fight for her, with citations. It’s right there behind his teeth.
body.else: He has known it since the first week: Catherine of Siena, the dyer’s daughter who bossed a pope. It’s right there behind his teeth.

response: “Catherine,” Jack says, under his breath, not quite under enough.

Wes hears it. Lena’s eyes come across the booth to Jack and go away again. Wes smiles, and says it anyway, the answer he brought with him: “Thérèse. It’s her name.” Lena turns her card. CATHERINE OF SIENA. Kevin, without looking up, docks Ohio a point on the napkin for conduct.
Last round. Laney to Lena: *The best thing he’s ever eaten?* “Mémère’s gumbo,” Lena says. “Yours, dawlin’,” says Wes. “That’s a lie, Wesley Arceneaux,” Lena says, “and it’s a sweet one.”
He keeps it in his mouth.

Wes is sure. “Thérèse,” he says. “It’s her name.” Lena turns her card over. CATHERINE OF SIENA, in capitals. Jack had it the whole time. Wes laughs at himself and says, “Well, she’s *named* for the other one.”
Last round. Laney to Lena: *The best thing he’s ever eaten?* “Mémère’s gumbo,” Lena says. “Yours, dawlin’,” says Wes. “That’s a lie, Wesley Arceneaux,” Lena says, “and it’s a sweet one.”

s05c.slug: SATURDAY · 2:31 PM · THE MADONNA INN, A PINK BOOTH
body: Laney taps the cake knife on a water glass. “Final round. Double points.” She reads it very slowly off the last card. “Wes. *What does Lena keep in her pocket?*”
Wes doesn’t hesitate. “Her rosary. Since tenth grade.”

Lena turns her card: ROSARY. Kevin writes. And Laney, the soul of surprise, pats the pocket of the oatmeal cardigan she is wearing, which is Lena’s, and lifts her eyebrows to the network. “And — oh! What’s *this*?”

It’s an Altoids tin, red and white, peppermint, from the gift shop of a pea-soup restaurant in Buellton, with RELIQUARY across the lid in the Buellton cashier’s Sharpie. Laney sets it down among the cake plates like a door prize.
“Delaney Rose,” Lena says.
“What’s a reliquary?” Becca asks.

Lena tells her, crisp, a lawyer reading the charge: Jack’s cigarettes, confiscated, one at a time, each one dated and labeled; she is curing him; the cure is going well. Becca reaches across the table and puts her hand on Lena’s wrist. “Oh, Lena, *thank you*!”
Wes picks up the tin. He opens it, and takes the slips out one at a time, in order, and reads them, and his lips move a little on the dates.

body.title: The Reliquary
body.text:
No. 1 · 8/29/09 · the Lighthouse.
No. 2 · 9/7/09 · Malibu · before breakfast, on a holiday.
No. 3 · 9/10/09 · the harbor · “confiscated and partially consumed by the Reliquarian”
No. 4 · 9/23/09 · the Delgado roof · a clove, by dispensation

body: He reads No. 3 out loud. “‘Confiscated and partially consumed by the Reliquarian.’” Kevin laughs, and Theo, and Laney. Wes laughs too. His comes in late, after everybody’s, and doesn’t stay long. “Partially consumed?”
“Medicinal,” Lena says.

body.title: Kevin’s napkin
body.text:
IDAHO 3 · NEW ORLEANS 3
OHIO −1 (CATHERINE, UNSOLICITED)
DELANEY: DISQUALIFIED (CONDUCT)

choices.text: “It’s a tax. Louisiana has a lot of them.”
response: “It’s a tax,” Jack says. “Louisiana has a lot of them.”

The booth laughs, Margot included, which Kevin notes on the napkin as a medical event. Wes laughs along, last. At four the return voyage leaves on schedule: Becca and Theo in the SL with the top down, the van behind. Wes rides up front again. In the way back Lena has the tin in the pocket of her dress now, and her hand over the pocket, the whole way down the 101.

choices.text: “She’s going to make me quit. Somebody has to.”
response: “She’s going to make me quit,” Jack says. “Somebody has to.”

Wes nods, slowly, turning the tin over in his big hand. “She made me quit dip in tenth grade.” He puts the slips back in order and closes the lid, and slides it across the table to Lena, not to Laney, and Lena puts it in the pocket of her dress. At four the return voyage leaves on schedule, the SL out front with Becca driving, the van behind.
“Becca’s taking over the collection,” Jack says.

Becca lights up. “I’ll get a *bigger tin*!” Jack looks at Lena and can’t read her face at all. Wes, for once, laughs right on time. Lena holds out her hand, and Wes gives her the tin, and she puts it in the pocket of her dress. At four the return voyage leaves on schedule, Becca and Theo in the SL, the rest of them in the van, Wes up front.
Jack says nothing.

Lena reaches across the cake plates and takes the tin out of Wes’s hand and puts it in her own pocket, the pocket of her dress, not Laney’s. No one says anything at all until Theo asks for the check. At four the return voyage leaves on schedule: the SL out front with its top down, the van behind, Wes up front, and the way back very quiet.
